nm_tortilla_flats.blurb: A short basalt band on the rim of Potrillo Canyon in White Rock, a little northwest of the Big Enchilada. Cliffs run roughly 40 to 50 feet with a broken ledge partway up, and most routes finish at a two-bolt anchor. The 17 climbs are nearly all trad with one top-rope line, from about 5.6 up to 5.10, with the bulk around 5.9 and below. It works best as a top-rope spot for newer climbers rather than a place to learn leading. The face is shaded into the early afternoon, so mornings are comfortable in summer, and it makes a quieter fallback when the neighbouring cliffs are busy.
nm_tortilla_flats.parking_note: Drive onto Estante Road and use the roadside pullout just beyond the fire hydrant, keeping clear of the hydrant, mailboxes and driveways.
nm_tortilla_flats.approach: Take the trail south from the road; at the split keep left and continue a few minutes to the rim, then use the cairned gullies at either end to reach the base.

nm_main_wall_5.blurb: The largest wall at Little River Wall, a few miles northwest of El Rito, sitting right beside the river at about 7,400 feet. The conglomerate face is around 90 to 100 feet tall, mostly just under vertical with a few steeper steps. All 17 routes are bolted sport lines, running from 5.8 up to 5.11, with a concentration around 5.10, so it suits climbers who are comfortable on moderate grades. A 60-meter rope covers most lines. The walls here face west and stay shady until around midday; a flat meadow at the base makes for a relaxed day, and crowds are light.

nm_chilly_willy_wall.blurb: A secluded, shady wall downstream from the main Las Conchas crags in the Jemez Mountains, at roughly 8,400 feet along the East Fork. It holds 17 climbs, mostly sport with a handful of trad lines, plus a boulder or two at the base. Grades span about 5.7 to 5.12, with the middle of the range around 5.10 and 5.11 and a good number of 5.12s for stronger climbers. Mornings are in shade and the afternoon brings filtered light through the trees, which keeps it cool in summer. The walk-in is short, with a river crossing on a log near the boardwalk.

nm_nascar_boulder.blurb: A boulder in the Ponderosa bouldering zone of the Jemez area, a short hike west of The Pond. Its signature feature is an overhanging, sloping traverse with many possible finishes, and the difficulty ramps up quickly the farther along it you go. The 17 problems cover a very wide spread, from easy warm-ups through the middle grades to a handful at V7 and above, with a few at the top end in double digits. It is a good stop for strong boulderers wanting a mix of power and sloper work, and the nearby boulders hold further undocumented problems.

nm_crystal_ship_and_glass_house.blurb: A tight cluster of about six good-quality granite boulders in the Three Gun area of the Sandia foothills near Albuquerque, set in two groups of three. The boulders sit close enough together that the spot can be sheltered or can funnel wind. The 17 problems run from V1 to V6, with most falling between V3 and V5, so it suits intermediate boulderers well. Expect knobby faces, a corridor between boulders and a long traverse. Grain in the foothills granite varies from excellent to crumbly, and the area sees fewer people than other nearby bouldering.

nm_chicken_little_area.blurb: The left-hand end of Cockscomb Crag, a basalt cliff in the Diablo Canyon area near Santa Fe. The trail arrives at a wall with three of the best lines, and the section holds 17 climbs, 11 sport and 6 trad, plus a top-rope. Grades run from about 5.8 to 5.12, mostly 5.9 through 5.11, with plenty for moderate climbers. The rock is generally solid and rewards crimping and side-pulling. Cockscomb is remote and quiet, and it is a poor winter choice because little sun reaches the wall from December through February. Spring and fall are the better seasons.

nm_cathedral_rock.blurb: The main crag of Pecos River Canyon, a roadside granite cliff in the national forest northeast of Santa Fe, at about 7,000 feet. Well-bolted sport routes are the draw, with 10 sport lines and 6 trad lines on mossy slabs and steep, roofed dihedrals, plus a boulder problem. Grades run from 5.8 into 5.13, with most between 5.9 and 5.11. The face points roughly west, so it is shaded in the morning and sunny later in the day. Because it sits right by the highway, belays happen on the shoulder and quiet is hard to find.

nm_north_rabbit_ear.blurb: A granite peak in the Organ Mountains above Las Cruces, reached by hiking up Rabbit Ears Canyon. This is alpine-style climbing, not sport: 16 trad routes and one aid line, with terrain from third and fourth class up to 5.11 and the majority at easier grades. The easiest ways up run through a steep chute and chimney system of chockstones, slabs and cracks, with loose rock and a long descent that involves rappels or a south-side scramble. It was once popular but now sees few visitors, so expect route-finding and a committing day.
